description: Application-owned, plain-language guidance for every metric exposed by the conservation explorer. Database definitions remain authoritative for calculations.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of all selected samples whose full haplotype pattern exactly matches the site-by-site consensus built from all samples. Unlike the complete-sequence consensus, this version keeps missing calls in the calculation, so '-' can become the consensus state at a position.
metrics.technical_definition: The consensus is built one position at a time using all selected samples. Missing calls are allowed to compete with amino acids, while a valid mixed call such as [A/V] contributes half to A and half to V. After the consensus pattern has been assembled, its frequency is the proportion of all normalized sample patterns that match that pattern exactly.
metrics.interpretation: A high value means one missing-aware pattern is common across the whole sample set. Interpret it together with call rate and missingness: a high frequency can reflect genuine sequence conservation, but it can also be influenced by a recurring missing-data pattern.
metrics.example: Suppose the all-sample consensus haplotype is A-K--V and 35 of 100 selected samples have exactly A-K--V. The metric is 35%. If '-' is the most common state at one position, that missing state is retained in the consensus.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, just over one third of all samples share the exact missing-aware consensus pattern. The value should not be read as 35% complete-sequence conservation because missing calls are part of the pattern.
metrics.help_tip: How often the all-sample, missing-aware consensus haplotype is actually observed. Higher values mean one overall pattern is common, but check missingness because '-' can be part of that pattern.

metrics.plain_language: Among complete haplotypes only, the fraction that exactly match the sequence made by taking the most common amino acid at each position. That site-by-site consensus does not have to be an observed haplotype.
metrics.technical_definition: First build the site-by-site consensus haplotype from callable amino-acid evidence. Then, among complete haplotypes only, calculate the proportion that match that consensus sequence exactly.
metrics.interpretation: A high value means one consensus haplotype represents a large share of the complete data. A value of 0 can occur when the site-wise consensus is a mosaic that no sample actually carries, so interpret it together with the top observed haplotype frequency.
metrics.example: Suppose 100 samples are selected, 90 have a complete haplotype, and the site-wise consensus is observed in 72 of those 90. The metric is 72/90 = 80%. If the consensus sequence is not present among the 90 complete observations, the value is 0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: An 80% value says the consensus sequence itself is very representative of complete observations. It does not say that 80% of all selected samples are complete.
metrics.help_tip: How often the site-by-site consensus sequence is actually observed as a complete haplotype. High values mean the consensus represents many complete observations; 0 can mean that consensus combination is never observed.

metrics.plain_language: Turns Shannon diversity into an intuitive count: the number of equally common haplotypes that would have the same diversity as the observed frequency distribution.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate Shannon diversity from the frequencies of complete haplotypes, then convert it to an effective count using exp(H). The result is the number of equally frequent haplotypes that would give the same Shannon diversity.
metrics.interpretation: 1 means essentially one haplotype is present. Larger values mean greater diversity. Unlike the raw number of observed haplotypes, rare types contribute only in proportion to their frequency, so a long tail of very rare types does not inflate the value as strongly.
metrics.example: Four equally common haplotypes (25%, 25%, 25%, 25%) give an effective number of 4. If the same four haplotypes occur at 70%, 10%, 10%, and 10%, the effective number falls to about 2.56.
metrics.example_interpretation: Both examples contain four observed haplotypes, but the second behaves, in diversity terms, more like about 2.6 equally common haplotypes because one type dominates.
metrics.help_tip: Diversity translated into an intuitive number of equally common haplotypes. A value of 4 means the observed diversity is equivalent to four haplotypes occurring at 25% each; higher means more diversity.

metrics.plain_language: The number of equally common haplotypes that would give the same Simpson diversity as the observed distribution. It emphasizes common types more strongly than the Shannon effective number.
metrics.technical_definition: Using complete haplotypes, square each frequency and add the squared values. The reciprocal of that sum, 1/Σp², is the effective Simpson count. This gives more weight to common haplotypes than to rare ones.
metrics.interpretation: 1 means one haplotype dominates completely; larger values mean more diversity. Because frequencies are squared, common haplotypes have more influence and very rare types have relatively little effect.
metrics.example: Four equally common haplotypes give 1/(4 × 0.25²) = 4. With frequencies 70%, 10%, 10%, 10%, the value is 1/(0.70² + 3×0.10²) ≈ 1.92.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 70/10/10/10 distribution still contains four haplotypes, but by this dominance-sensitive measure it behaves like only about 1.9 equally common haplotypes.
metrics.help_tip: The effective number of common haplotypes, with extra weight on the most frequent ones. A value of 2 means the distribution behaves roughly like two equally common haplotypes; higher means more diversity.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥1 missing call within the block.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count the missing '-' calls in the block. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 1 missing call.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean missing data affect fewer samples. Thresholded versions help distinguish occasional isolated missing calls from samples with more substantial missingness.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 12 contain ≥1 missing call, the value is 12%. A stricter threshold can only stay the same or decrease.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 12% means 88% of selected samples do not meet this missingness threshold.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 1 missing call in the block. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥5 missing calls within the block.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count the missing '-' calls in the block. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 5 missing calls.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean missing data affect fewer samples. Thresholded versions help distinguish occasional isolated missing calls from samples with more substantial missingness.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 12 contain ≥5 missing calls, the value is 12%. A stricter threshold can only stay the same or decrease.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 12% means 88% of selected samples do not meet this missingness threshold.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 5 missing calls in the block. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with >5 missing calls within the block.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count the missing '-' calls in the block. The metric is the proportion of samples with more than 5 missing calls.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean missing data affect fewer samples. Thresholded versions help distinguish occasional isolated missing calls from samples with more substantial missingness.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 12 contain >5 missing calls, the value is 12%. A stricter threshold can only stay the same or decrease.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 12% means 88% of selected samples do not meet this missingness threshold.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with more than 5 missing calls in the block. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥1 mixed callable call within the block. A mixed call records more than one possible amino acid, such as [A/V], rather than being missing.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count callable positions in the block that contain more than one possible amino acid. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 1 mixed call.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean mixed infection or call ambiguity affects more samples at this threshold. Mixed calls remain callable and are therefore different from missing or unresolved calls.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 18 contain ≥1 mixed callable call, the value is 18%. A threshold of ≥5 mixed calls would normally be much lower than a threshold of ≥1.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, mixed calls are present at this level in 18% of samples; the metric does not say that 18% of individual positions are mixed.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 1 mixed amino-acid call in the block. Higher values mean mixed calls affect more samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥1 non-callable position in the block. Non-callable positions are missing or unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count positions in the block that are missing or unresolved. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 1 non-callable position.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more samples have usable sequence information across the region. This combines missing and unresolved calls into one sample-level measure.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 15 contain ≥1 non-callable position, the value is 15%; the other 85 samples fall below that non-callable threshold.
metrics.example_interpretation: This tells you how many samples are affected, not how many total positions are non-callable.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 1 non-callable positions (missing or unresolved) in the block. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of amino-acid positions in the block where the second most common residue has any detectable frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the block, identify the second most common amino acid using fractional residue frequencies. A position is counted as polymorphic when that second residue has any non-zero frequency; the metric is the fraction of positions that meet this rule.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position block, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. The corresponding fractions are 16%, 10%, and 4%; for this metric the relevant value is 8/50 = 16%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of positions in the block where any alternative amino acid is observed, even if very rare. Higher values mean polymorphism is spread across more positions.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of amino-acid positions in the block where the second most common residue has at least 1% frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the block, identify the second most common amino acid using fractional residue frequencies. A position is counted as polymorphic when that second residue has at least 1% frequency; the metric is the fraction of positions that meet this rule.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position block, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. The corresponding fractions are 16%, 10%, and 4%; for this metric the relevant value is 5/50 = 10%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of positions in the block where an alternative amino acid reaches at least 1% frequency. This ignores rarer alternatives and highlights more established variation.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of amino-acid positions in the block where the second most common residue has at least 5% frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the block, identify the second most common amino acid using fractional residue frequencies. A position is counted as polymorphic when that second residue has at least 5% frequency; the metric is the fraction of positions that meet this rule.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position block, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. The corresponding fractions are 16%, 10%, and 4%; for this metric the relevant value is 2/50 = 4%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of positions in the block where an alternative amino acid reaches at least 5% frequency. This ignores rarer alternatives and highlights more established variation.

metrics.display_name: Fraction of Sites with a Singleton Residue
metrics.plain_language: The fraction of positions in the block where at least one amino acid is seen in exactly one selected sample. Presence inside a mixed call still counts as presence in that one sample.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the block, check whether any amino acid is present in exactly one sample. A residue seen inside a mixed call still counts as present in that sample. The metric is the fraction of positions containing at least one such singleton residue.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean rare, sample-specific amino-acid variants are spread across more positions. Singleton-rich regions can look polymorphic even when recurrent variants are uncommon.
metrics.example: If a 50-position block has singleton residues at 6 positions, the fraction is 6/50 = 12%. A V seen only once inside [A/V] still makes that site singleton-positive; V seen in two samples does not.
metrics.example_interpretation: This highlights the rarest end of the variation spectrum and complements the ≥1% or ≥5% polymorphism metrics.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of positions in the block that contain an amino acid seen in only one sample. Higher values mean rare one-off variants are spread across more positions.

metrics.plain_language: The probability that two complete haplotypes drawn from the sample are different, with a small correction for finite sample size.
metrics.technical_definition: Using complete haplotypes only, calculate 1 − Σp² from their observed frequencies and apply the finite-sample correction n/(n−1). This estimates the probability that two randomly chosen complete haplotypes are different.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 0 mean most complete observations are the same haplotype; values near 1 mean two randomly chosen complete observations are very likely to be different. Hd captures both richness and frequency balance, but it does not tell you how many amino-acid positions differ.
metrics.example: With two haplotypes at 90% and 10%, the uncorrected value is 1−(0.9²+0.1²)=0.18. At 50% and 50%, it is 0.50. The stored Hd is slightly higher after multiplying by n/(n−1).
metrics.example_interpretation: Two equally common haplotypes produce much more diversity than a 90/10 split, even though both blocks contain exactly two observed types.
metrics.help_tip: The chance that two randomly chosen complete haplotypes are different. 0 means they are all the same; values closer to 1 mean two random haplotypes are very likely to differ.

metrics.plain_language: Measures how unevenly frequency is distributed across the observed haplotype types. A value of 0 means all observed types are equally frequent; larger values mean a few types dominate.
metrics.technical_definition: Apply the standard Gini coefficient to the positive complete haplotype frequencies. Only types that are actually observed are included; absent types with zero frequency are ignored.
metrics.interpretation: Low Gini means the observed haplotype types have similar frequencies. High Gini means frequency is concentrated in a small number of types. Unlike a diversity index, Gini focuses specifically on inequality among the types that are present.
metrics.example: Four types at 25%, 25%, 25%, 25% have Gini = 0. Four types at 70%, 10%, 10%, 10% have Gini ≈ 0.45; at 97%, 1%, 1%, 1% it is ≈ 0.72.
metrics.example_interpretation: The number of observed types is unchanged, but the Gini rises as one type becomes increasingly dominant.
metrics.help_tip: How unequal the frequencies of the observed haplotypes are. 0 means all types are equally common; higher values mean one or a few types dominate.

metrics.plain_language: The average pairwise amino-acid difference between complete haplotypes, expressed as a fraction of the block length so regions of different lengths are comparable.
metrics.technical_definition: Compare every pair of complete haplotypes, count the amino-acid positions at which each pair differs, and average those distances. Divide that mean by the block length so values from regions of different lengths are directly comparable.
metrics.interpretation: 0 means complete sequences are identical. A value of 0.10 means a typical pair differs at about 10% of positions. This is more comparable across block/window lengths than the raw pairwise distance.
metrics.example: An average of 2 differences in a 20-AA region gives 2/20 = 0.10. The same 2 differences in a 100-AA region give 0.02.
metrics.example_interpretation: The absolute number of differences is the same, but variation is much denser in the 20-AA region.
metrics.help_tip: The average pairwise amino-acid difference expressed as a fraction of sequence length. For example, 0.10 means two complete haplotypes differ at about 10% of positions on average.

metrics.plain_language: For two randomly chosen complete haplotypes, the average number of amino-acid positions at which their sequences differ.
metrics.technical_definition: Compare every unordered pair of complete haplotype observations, count how many amino-acid positions differ in each pair, and take the average number of differences.
metrics.interpretation: 0 means all complete haplotypes are identical. Larger values mean complete sequences differ at more positions on average. Because this is an absolute count, longer regions can naturally have larger values.
metrics.example: If three complete haplotypes have pairwise distances of 1, 2, and 3 amino acids, the mean distance is (1+2+3)/3 = 2 AA.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 2 means a typical pair of complete haplotypes differs at about two positions.
metrics.help_tip: The average number of amino-acid positions at which two complete haplotypes differ. Larger values mean the sequences are typically farther apart.

metrics.plain_language: For each sample, calculate the fraction of positions in the block that are callable, then average those fractions across samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, calculate the proportion of positions in the block that are callable, then average those per-sample proportions.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean samples are, on average, well covered by usable calls. Because each sample contributes equally, one sample does not get extra weight simply because it has more callable positions.
metrics.example: If three samples have call rates of 100%, 90%, and 80%, the mean sample call rate is 90%.
metrics.example_interpretation: A 90% value means the average sample has callable information at about nine out of every ten positions.
metrics.help_tip: For each sample, the fraction of positions in the block that are callable, averaged across samples. Higher values mean more complete sequence information overall.

metrics.plain_language: For each sample, the fraction of block positions marked missing (-), averaged across all selected samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, calculate the proportion of positions in the block marked missing ('-'), then average those proportions across samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values are better. A value of 0 means no missing calls; 0.05 means the average sample is missing 5% of positions.
metrics.example: If three samples have missing fractions of 0%, 5%, and 10%, the average missing fraction is 5%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The average sample is missing about one position in twenty, although individual samples may be better or worse.
metrics.help_tip: The average fraction of positions in the block that are explicitly missing in each sample. Lower values mean less missing sequence data.

metrics.display_name: Average Mixed Fraction per Sample (Callable Positions)
metrics.plain_language: For each sample, calculate what fraction of its callable block positions are mixed calls such as [A/V], then average those fractions across samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, look only at callable positions in the block and calculate what fraction are mixed calls. The reported value is the average of those per-sample fractions.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean mixed calls occupy more of the callable sequence in a typical sample. Each sample contributes equally, regardless of how many callable positions it has.
metrics.example: If two samples have mixed fractions of 0% and 20% among their callable positions, the mean is 10%, even if one sample has many more callable positions than the other.
metrics.example_interpretation: This describes the typical sample. It can differ from the pooled mixed fraction, which gives more weight to samples with more callable positions.
metrics.help_tip: Among callable positions, the average fraction that are mixed within each sample. Higher values mean samples more often contain evidence for multiple amino acids at the same position.

metrics.plain_language: For each sample, the fraction of block positions that are missing or unresolved, averaged across selected samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, calculate the fraction of positions in the block that are missing or unresolved, then average across samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more complete usable sequence information. This is broader than missing fraction because it also counts unresolved calls.
metrics.example: If sample non-callable fractions are 2%, 4%, and 9%, the average is 5%.
metrics.example_interpretation: On average, 5% of positions per sample cannot be used as resolved amino-acid calls.
metrics.help_tip: The average fraction of positions in the block that cannot be used because they are missing or unresolved. Lower values mean cleaner sequence data.

metrics.plain_language: For each sample, the fraction of block positions carrying unresolved non-missing markers such as ! or *, averaged across samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, calculate the fraction of positions in the block that are unresolved but not missing, then average across samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values are better. High values indicate that sequence information is present but cannot be represented as a resolved canonical amino-acid call.
metrics.example: If three samples have unresolved fractions of 0%, 3%, and 6%, the average is 3%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The average sample has unresolved evidence at about 3% of positions, separately from explicitly missing '-' calls.
metrics.help_tip: The average fraction of positions in the block carrying unresolved calls rather than a usable amino acid. Lower values mean fewer ambiguous technical calls.

metrics.plain_language: The middle per-sample call rate for the block: half the samples have a call rate at or below it and half at or above it.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate the call rate separately for every sample across the block, then take the median rather than the mean.
metrics.interpretation: Higher is better. The median is resistant to a small number of very poorly called samples, so comparing it with the mean can reveal outliers.
metrics.example: If three samples have call rates of 100%, 95%, and 20%, the median is 95% while the mean is about 72%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Most samples are well called, but one poor sample drags down the mean; the median makes that contrast obvious.
metrics.help_tip: The typical per-sample call rate for the block: half of samples are above it and half below. Higher values mean a typical sample has more usable sequence data.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of all selected samples with the most common normalized haplotype pattern, counting complete patterns and patterns that contain missing, unresolved, or mixed calls.
metrics.technical_definition: Treat each selected sample's full haplotype call pattern as an observed pattern, including missing, unresolved, or mixed calls. After normalizing their representation, identify the most common pattern and divide its count by the total number of selected samples.
metrics.interpretation: A high value means one exact call pattern is common across the whole selected cohort. Because incomplete patterns are allowed, a high value can sometimes reflect a recurrent missing or mixed-call pattern rather than a common biological sequence.
metrics.example: In 100 samples, suppose the most common pattern occurs 42 times and contains one missing position, while the most common complete haplotype occurs 35 times. This metric is 42%, whereas the complete-{seq} frequency metric would be based only on complete observations.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 42% value describes the most repeated observed call pattern, not necessarily the most common fully resolved biological sequence.
metrics.help_tip: The frequency of the most common haplotype call pattern when every sample is included, even those with missing or mixed calls. Useful for seeing the dominant observed pattern without requiring complete sequences.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of sample-by-position calls in the block that are callable: neither missing nor unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: Count every sample-by-position call in the block that is neither missing nor unresolved. Mixed calls are included because they are still callable.
metrics.interpretation: Higher counts mean more usable sequence evidence, but the value scales with both cohort size and region length.
metrics.example: With 100 samples and a 20-position block, there are 2,000 possible calls. If 1,940 are callable, this metric is 1,940.
metrics.example_interpretation: The dataset provides usable amino-acid information for 97% of all possible sample-by-position calls in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of usable amino-acid calls across all samples and positions in the block. Larger counts usually mean more data, but also reflect cohort and region size.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples whose entire block contains only unambiguous canonical amino acids—no missing, unresolved, or mixed calls.
metrics.technical_definition: Count sample observations whose entire block contains one unambiguous canonical amino acid at every position. Any missing, unresolved, or mixed position makes the observation incomplete.
metrics.interpretation: Higher counts provide a larger evidence base for complete-haplotype frequency and diversity metrics. The count can be much smaller than n_samples if mixed or incomplete calls are common.
metrics.example: If 1,000 samples are selected and 860 have an unambiguous canonical call at every position, there are 860 complete haplotype observations.
metrics.example_interpretation: Complete-haplotype metrics are based on these 860 observations, not automatically on all 1,000 samples.
metrics.help_tip: The number of samples with a complete block haplotype containing only unambiguous amino acids. These are the observations used for exact haplotype-frequency and diversity calculations.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples with no missing or unresolved positions anywhere in the block. Mixed calls are allowed.
metrics.technical_definition: Count sample observations with no missing or unresolved positions anywhere in the block. Mixed calls are allowed because they still contain callable amino-acid information.
metrics.interpretation: This is a less strict completeness measure than complete haplotype observations because mixed calls are allowed. A large gap between the two counts points to mixed calls rather than missingness.
metrics.example: If 1,000 samples include 920 fully callable haplotypes, but only 860 are complete unambiguous haplotypes, then 60 observations are fully callable yet contain at least one mixed call.
metrics.example_interpretation: The difference between fully callable and fully complete observations helps separate mixed-call ambiguity from missing/unresolved data.
metrics.help_tip: The number of block sequences with no missing or unresolved positions. Mixed calls are allowed, so this can be larger than the number of complete unambiguous haplotypes.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of calls in the block marked missing (-).
metrics.technical_definition: Count all positions marked missing ('-') across the selected samples and all positions in the block.
metrics.interpretation: Lower is better, but the raw count depends on sample number and region length.
metrics.example: In 2,000 possible sample-by-position calls, 40 missing '-' calls give this metric a value of 40.
metrics.example_interpretation: Forty individual calls are missing; this does not tell you whether they are concentrated in a few samples or spread across many.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of missing calls across the block. Lower counts mean less missing data, but compare counts only across similarly sized cohorts and regions.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of callable positions in the block with more than one possible amino acid, such as [A/V].
metrics.technical_definition: Count all callable positions in the block that contain more than one possible canonical amino acid, such as [A/V].
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean more mixed-call evidence, but the count also grows with cohort size and region length.
metrics.example: If 30 of 1,940 callable sample-by-position calls are mixed, this metric is 30.
metrics.example_interpretation: There are 30 mixed calls in total; the pooled mixed fraction would express this relative to the 1,940 callable calls.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of callable positions containing multiple possible amino acids across the block. Higher counts mean mixed calls are more common, but counts depend on dataset size.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of calls in the block that are missing or unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: Count all missing calls plus all unresolved non-missing calls across the selected samples and positions in the block.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more usable sequence evidence. The raw count depends on cohort size and region length.
metrics.example: If a block contains 40 missing calls and 10 unresolved calls, the non-callable count is 50.
metrics.example_interpretation: The combined value shows total unusable calls; separate missing and unresolved counts show why they are unusable.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of missing or unresolved calls across the block. Lower counts mean cleaner data, but counts depend on cohort and region size.

metrics.plain_language: The number of QC-pass samples contributing to this metric in the current stratum.
metrics.technical_definition: Count the QC-pass samples included in the currently selected population or geographic stratum.
metrics.interpretation: Larger sample sizes usually make frequency estimates more stable, but sample count is not itself a measure of conservation or quality.
metrics.example: If the current country/year stratum contains 1,250 QC-pass samples, this metric is 1,250.
metrics.example_interpretation: All percentages and counts for this stratum should be interpreted in the context of these 1,250 contributing samples.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected QC-passing samples contributing to this block. Use it to judge how much sample support underlies the other metrics.

metrics.plain_language: The number of distinct complete haplotype types observed in exactly one selected sample.
metrics.technical_definition: Among the distinct complete haplotype sequences, count how many are observed in exactly one sample.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a larger rare tail of one-off complete haplotypes. Singleton counts are especially sensitive to sample size and possible sequencing/calling artefacts.
metrics.example: If 20 distinct complete haplotypes are observed and 7 occur in only one sample each, this metric is 7.
metrics.example_interpretation: Seven of the observed haplotype types are unique to single samples; the remaining 13 occur at least twice.
metrics.help_tip: The number of distinct complete haplotype types seen in only one sample. Many singletons can indicate a long tail of rare sequence variants.

metrics.plain_language: The number of amino-acid positions in the block where the second most common residue has any detectable frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the block, look at the second most common amino acid. Count the positions where that alternative residue has any non-zero frequency.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position block, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. For this metric the count is 8.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The number of positions in the block where any alternative amino acid is observed, even if only once. More sites means variation is distributed across more positions.

metrics.plain_language: The number of amino-acid positions in the block where the second most common residue has at least 1% frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the block, look at the second most common amino acid. Count the positions where that alternative residue has at least 1% frequency.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position block, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. For this metric the count is 5.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The number of positions in the block where an alternative amino acid reaches at least 1% frequency. This focuses on variation that is more than extremely rare.

metrics.plain_language: The number of amino-acid positions in the block where the second most common residue has at least 5% frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the block, look at the second most common amino acid. Count the positions where that alternative residue has at least 5% frequency.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position block, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. For this metric the count is 2.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The number of positions in the block where an alternative amino acid reaches at least 5% frequency. This focuses on variation that is more than extremely rare.

metrics.plain_language: The number of positions in the block where at least one amino acid is seen in exactly one selected sample. Presence inside a mixed call still counts as presence in that one sample.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the block, check whether any amino acid appears in exactly one sample, including appearances inside mixed calls. Count the positions that contain at least one such singleton residue.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean rare, sample-specific amino-acid variants are spread across more positions. Singleton-rich regions can look polymorphic even when recurrent variants are uncommon.
metrics.example: If a 50-position block has singleton residues at 6 positions, the count is 6. A V seen only once inside [A/V] still makes that site singleton-positive; V seen in two samples does not.
metrics.example_interpretation: This highlights the rarest end of the variation spectrum and complements the ≥1% or ≥5% polymorphism metrics.
metrics.help_tip: The number of positions in the block containing an amino acid seen in only one sample. This highlights sites carrying very rare variants.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of sample-by-position calls represented in the block.
metrics.technical_definition: Count all sample-by-position entries in the block. This is the number of selected samples multiplied by the number of positions in the block.
metrics.interpretation: This is mainly a denominator/evidence-size metric rather than a conservation metric.
metrics.example: With 100 selected samples and a 20-position block, there are 100 × 20 = 2,000 total calls.
metrics.example_interpretation: This is the maximum pool from which callable, missing, mixed, and unresolved call counts are drawn.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of sample-by-position calls in the block, before separating callable, missing, mixed, or unresolved calls.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of calls in the block that contain exactly one standard amino acid.
metrics.technical_definition: Count calls in the block that contain exactly one standard amino acid. Mixed, missing, and unresolved calls are not included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher counts mean more directly resolved amino-acid evidence, but raw counts depend on sample number and region length.
metrics.example: If 2,000 total calls include 1,900 single canonical residues, 40 mixed calls, and 60 non-callable calls, this metric is 1,900.
metrics.example_interpretation: Most calls are fully resolved to one standard amino acid; mixed and non-callable calls are excluded from this count.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of clear, single-amino-acid calls across all samples and positions in the block. Higher counts mean more directly interpretable sequence data.

metrics.plain_language: The number of different complete haplotype sequences observed among selected samples.
metrics.technical_definition: Among complete, unambiguous haplotype observations, collapse identical sequences together and count the number of distinct sequences.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean greater observed richness, but this raw count increases with sample size and can be inflated by rare singletons.
metrics.example: If 500 complete observations contain 12 different haplotype sequences, this metric is 12. If 8 of those 12 occur only once, richness is high but much of it is rare.
metrics.example_interpretation: A count of 12 tells you how many types were seen, not whether they are common or evenly distributed.
metrics.help_tip: The number of distinct complete haplotype sequences observed in the block. More types mean greater haplotype richness, although this count also grows with sample size.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of non-missing calls in the block that remain unresolved, for example calls represented by markers such as ! or *.
metrics.technical_definition: Count non-missing calls in the block that are marked unresolved rather than assigned a usable amino-acid state.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values are better. This separates unresolved sequence information from explicit missing '-' calls.
metrics.example: If 2,000 total calls contain 10 unresolved non-missing calls, this metric is 10.
metrics.example_interpretation: Ten positions contain sequence information that cannot be represented as a resolved amino-acid call.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of unresolved, non-missing calls across the block. Lower counts mean fewer ambiguous technical calls.

metrics.plain_language: Shows how evenly the observed haplotypes share the total frequency, scaled from 0 toward 1. It asks about balance, not simply how many types exist.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate Shannon diversity H for the observed haplotypes, then divide it by ln(S), where S is the number of observed types. This rescales diversity relative to the maximum possible value if those observed types were equally frequent.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 mean the observed haplotypes are similarly frequent. Lower values mean one or a few types dominate. Two regions can have the same number of observed types but very different evenness.
metrics.example: With four types at 25% each, Pielou evenness is 1.00. With the same four types at 70%, 10%, 10%, 10%, it is about 0.68.
metrics.example_interpretation: Both examples have four observed types, but the first is perfectly balanced whereas the second is strongly dominated by one type.
metrics.help_tip: How evenly the observed haplotypes are represented. 1 means all observed types are equally frequent; lower values mean some types are much more common than others.

metrics.plain_language: Across all callable sample-by-position calls in the block, the fraction that are mixed calls such as [A/V].
metrics.technical_definition: Pool all callable sample-by-position calls in the block. The metric is the number of mixed calls divided by the total number of callable calls, so samples with more callable positions contribute more observations.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a larger share of all usable calls are mixed. Samples with more callable positions contribute more calls, unlike the mean per-sample mixed fraction.
metrics.example: Suppose sample A has 100 callable positions with 10 mixed calls and sample B has 10 callable positions with 0 mixed calls. The pooled fraction is 10/110 = 9.1%, while the mean of the two sample fractions is (10%+0%)/2 = 5%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The pooled metric is higher because the sample with more callable data contributes more weight.
metrics.help_tip: The overall share of callable sample-by-position calls in the block that are mixed. Higher values mean mixed infections or ambiguous within-sample residue calls are more common.

metrics.plain_language: Among complete haplotypes, the fraction that exactly match the 3D7 reference sequence across the whole block.
metrics.technical_definition: Among complete haplotype observations only, count those that match the 3D7 reference sequence exactly and divide by the total number of complete observations. Sequences with missing, unresolved, or mixed calls are excluded.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 mean the 3D7 haplotype is highly representative of the complete observations; low values mean most complete haplotypes differ from 3D7. This measures reference representativeness, not overall diversity.
metrics.example: If 90 samples have complete haplotypes and 72 are identical to 3D7, the frequency is 72/90 = 80%. If another 10 selected samples are incomplete, they do not enter this denominator.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, 3D7 represents four out of five complete observations, but the metric says nothing about how the remaining 20% are distributed among other types.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete haplotypes that exactly match the 3D7 reference sequence. High values mean the reference form is common in this population.

metrics.plain_language: Summarizes diversity by combining how many haplotypes are observed with how evenly their frequencies are distributed. More types and a more even distribution both increase the value.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate H = −Σ(p × ln p) from the positive frequencies of the observed complete haplotypes, using the natural logarithm. Both the number of types and how evenly they are represented affect the value.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean greater diversity, but the number is not itself a count and its maximum depends on how many types are present. For a more intuitive scale, use the corresponding effective-number metric where available.
metrics.example: Two equally frequent types (50%/50%) give H = 0.693 nats. Four equally frequent types give H = 1.386. Two types at 90%/10% give only H ≈ 0.325.
metrics.example_interpretation: Shannon diversity increases both when more types are present and when frequencies become more balanced.
metrics.help_tip: A diversity score that increases when there are more haplotypes and when their frequencies are more even. 0 means only one complete haplotype is observed; higher values mean greater diversity.

metrics.display_name: Singleton Share of Complete Haplotype Types
metrics.plain_language: Among the distinct complete haplotype types observed, the fraction that occur in exactly one selected sample.
metrics.technical_definition: Count distinct complete haplotype types seen in exactly one sample and divide by the total number of distinct complete haplotype types.
metrics.interpretation: High values mean much of the observed richness consists of one-off haplotypes; low values mean most distinct types recur in multiple samples.
metrics.example: If 20 distinct complete haplotypes are observed and 7 are singletons, the fraction is 7/20 = 35%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Although 20 types were observed, more than a third of those types are represented by only one sample each.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of distinct complete haplotype types that occur only once. A high value means much of the observed sequence richness consists of rare, one-sample types.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete haplotype observations accounted for by the 10 most common complete haplotype types.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete haplotype types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 10. If fewer than 10 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common haplotypes covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-haplotype frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-10 coverage is 100.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 10 most common complete haplotypes together represent 100.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete haplotype observations covered by the 10 most common haplotypes together. Higher values mean a small set of sequences captures more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete haplotype observations accounted for by the 1 most common complete haplotype type.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete haplotype types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 1. If fewer than 1 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common haplotypes covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-haplotype frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-1 coverage is 40.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 1 most common complete haplotype together represent 40.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete haplotype observations explained by the single most common haplotype. Higher values mean one sequence covers more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete haplotype observations accounted for by the 2 most common complete haplotype types.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete haplotype types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 2. If fewer than 2 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common haplotypes covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-haplotype frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-2 coverage is 65.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 2 most common complete haplotypes together represent 65.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete haplotype observations covered by the 2 most common haplotypes together. Higher values mean a small set of sequences captures more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete haplotype observations accounted for by the 3 most common complete haplotype types.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete haplotype types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 3. If fewer than 3 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common haplotypes covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-haplotype frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-3 coverage is 80.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 3 most common complete haplotypes together represent 80.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete haplotype observations covered by the 3 most common haplotypes together. Higher values mean a small set of sequences captures more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete haplotype observations accounted for by the 5 most common complete haplotype types.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete haplotype types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 5. If fewer than 5 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common haplotypes covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-haplotype frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-5 coverage is 95.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 5 most common complete haplotypes together represent 95.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete haplotype observations covered by the 5 most common haplotypes together. Higher values mean a small set of sequences captures more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: Among complete haplotypes, the fraction belonging to the single most common observed haplotype.
metrics.technical_definition: Among complete haplotype observations only, identify the most common distinct sequence and report its frequency. Observations containing missing, unresolved, or mixed calls do not contribute.
metrics.interpretation: A high value means one haplotype dominates the complete observations. A low value means the observations are spread across several haplotypes. The most common haplotype is not necessarily the 3D7 or site-wise consensus sequence.
metrics.example: If 90 complete haplotypes contain 54 copies of type A, 18 of type B, and 18 across other types, the value is 54/90 = 60%. A second block with frequencies 30%, 25%, 20%, … would have a much lower top frequency despite having the same number of complete observations.
metrics.example_interpretation: The first block is dominated by one haplotype; the second is more evenly split among several haplotypes.
metrics.help_tip: The frequency of the single most common complete haplotype. A high value means one sequence dominates; a low value means the population is spread across several sequences.

metrics.plain_language: The total amino-acid weight used as the denominator for fractional residue frequencies at this locus. Each usable sample contributes one unit of weight, even when that unit is split across residues in a mixed call.
metrics.technical_definition: Each callable sample contributes a total weight of 1 to the amino-acid frequencies. A single-residue call gives all of that weight to one amino acid; a mixed call splits the weight equally among its possible canonical residues. Missing or otherwise non-contributing calls add no weight.
metrics.interpretation: This is an evidence denominator, not a diversity measure. Larger values mean more sample information contributes to residue-frequency estimates.
metrics.example: Calls A, [A/V], and '-' contribute total allele weight 1 + 1 + 0 = 2. The residue weights are A = 1.5 and V = 0.5.
metrics.example_interpretation: The mixed call contributes one sample's worth of evidence, shared equally between its two possible residues.
metrics.help_tip: The total callable sample weight used to calculate amino-acid frequencies at this site. Each callable sample contributes one unit, with mixed calls splitting that unit across their possible residues.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples with one clearly resolved canonical amino acid at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Count samples with exactly one unambiguous canonical amino acid at this locus. Mixed, missing, unresolved, and non-allelic ambiguous calls are excluded.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values provide more direct evidence for the residue distribution, but the raw count also depends on cohort size.
metrics.example: Among 100 samples, if 90 have a single canonical residue, 5 are mixed, and 5 are missing/unresolved, this metric is 90.
metrics.example_interpretation: Ninety samples provide an unambiguous one-residue observation at the locus.
metrics.help_tip: The number of samples with one clear canonical amino acid at this site. Mixed, missing, and unresolved calls do not count.

metrics.plain_language: Measures how unevenly frequency is distributed across the observed amino-acid types. A value of 0 means all observed types are equally frequent; larger values mean a few types dominate.
metrics.technical_definition: Apply the standard Gini coefficient to the positive amino-acid frequencies. Only types that are actually observed are included; absent types with zero frequency are ignored.
metrics.interpretation: Low Gini means the observed amino-acid types have similar frequencies. High Gini means frequency is concentrated in a small number of types. Unlike a diversity index, Gini focuses specifically on inequality among the types that are present.
metrics.example: Four types at 25%, 25%, 25%, 25% have Gini = 0. Four types at 70%, 10%, 10%, 10% have Gini ≈ 0.45; at 97%, 1%, 1%, 1% it is ≈ 0.72.
metrics.example_interpretation: The number of observed types is unchanged, but the Gini rises as one type becomes increasingly dominant.
metrics.help_tip: How unequal the amino-acid frequencies are at this site. 0 means the observed residues are equally common; higher values mean one or a few residues dominate.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with a callable amino-acid result at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Divide the number of callable samples at this locus by the total number of selected samples. A call is callable when it is neither missing nor unresolved.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 indicate strong coverage of usable calls. Low call rate weakens confidence in allele-frequency and diversity estimates for the locus.
metrics.example: If 970 of 1,000 selected samples are callable, the call rate is 97%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Residue-based metrics at this locus are supported by usable calls from almost the entire cohort.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with a usable amino-acid call at this site. Higher values mean stronger data coverage at the position.

metrics.plain_language: The fractional frequency of the most common amino acid at this locus, after splitting mixed calls across their possible residues.
metrics.technical_definition: First convert callable observations into fractional amino-acid weights, splitting valid mixed calls equally across their possible residues. Divide each residue's weight by the total callable weight; the largest resulting frequency is the consensus frequency.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 indicate strong residue-level conservation. Lower values mean substantial support for alternative amino acids.
metrics.example: Calls A, A, and [A/V] give weights A = 2.5 and V = 0.5, so the consensus frequency is 2.5/3 = 83.3%. By comparison, A and [A/V] alone give 75%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The first locus is more strongly dominated by A because the mixed call contributes only half its weight to V.
metrics.help_tip: The frequency of the most common amino acid at this site after mixed calls are split across their possible residues. Higher values mean the site is more strongly dominated by one residue.

metrics.plain_language: Whether two or more amino acids share the highest fractional frequency at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Compare the fractional frequencies of all observed amino acids. The value is true when two or more residues share the highest frequency, so there is no unique consensus residue.
metrics.interpretation: True means there is no unique consensus residue in the selected sample group.
metrics.example: If A and V each have 50% fractional frequency, the value is true. At 51% A and 49% V, it is false.
metrics.example_interpretation: A tiny shift from 50/50 to 51/49 creates a unique consensus, so also inspect the actual frequencies.
metrics.help_tip: Whether two or more amino acids are tied for the highest frequency at this site. If true, there is no single most common residue.

metrics.plain_language: Whether the 3D7 reference amino acid appears in at least one selected sample at this locus, including as one option inside a mixed call.
metrics.technical_definition: Check whether the 3D7 reference amino acid appears in at least one selected sample. An occurrence inside a valid mixed call counts as present.
metrics.interpretation: False means the 3D7 residue is absent from the selected sample group at this locus. True only establishes presence, not commonness.
metrics.example: If the 3D7 residue is A and the calls are V, V, and [A/V], the value is true even though no sample has an unambiguous A call.
metrics.example_interpretation: The reference residue is represented in the data, but it may still be rare.
metrics.help_tip: Whether the 3D7 reference amino acid appears in at least one selected sample at this site, including as one possibility within a mixed call.

metrics.plain_language: The probability that two independent amino-acid draws from this locus are different, using fractional residue frequencies.
metrics.technical_definition: Using fractional amino-acid frequencies, calculate He = 1 − Σp². This is the probability that two independent residue draws from the locus are different.
metrics.interpretation: 0 means the locus is completely conserved in the observed residue distribution. Larger values mean more residue diversity; the maximum depends on how many residue types are present.
metrics.example: A 90%/10% split gives He = 0.18, while a 50%/50% split gives He = 0.50.
metrics.example_interpretation: Both loci have two residues, but the balanced 50/50 locus is much more diverse because two random draws differ half the time.
metrics.help_tip: The chance that two random amino-acid draws from this site are different. 0 means the site is uniform; higher values mean more residue diversity.

metrics.plain_language: Whether any amino acid at this locus is seen in exactly one selected sample. A residue inside a mixed call counts as present in that sample.
metrics.technical_definition: For each canonical amino acid, count how many samples contain it, including occurrences inside mixed calls. The value is true if any residue appears in exactly one sample.
metrics.interpretation: True flags a one-off rare residue. It does not imply that the locus has common polymorphism.
metrics.example: If V appears only once, in a single [A/V] call, the flag is true. If V appears in two samples, it is false unless another residue is a singleton.
metrics.example_interpretation: A site can be polymorphic because of a single rare observation, which is different from having a recurrent alternative allele.
metrics.help_tip: Whether any amino acid at this site is seen in exactly one selected sample. This flags a very rare, sample-specific residue.

metrics.plain_language: Whether the second most common amino acid at this locus has any positive frequency.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank the fractional amino-acid frequencies. The locus is polymorphic when a second residue is present at any non-zero frequency.
metrics.interpretation: True means the locus passes this polymorphism threshold. The 'any' threshold is sensitive to single rare observations; 1% and 5% thresholds require progressively more common alternatives.
metrics.example: If the second residue frequency is 0.2%, this flag is true under the stated threshold. A locus with a second residue at 0.8% fails the ≥1% rule and therefore also fails the ≥5% rule.
metrics.example_interpretation: Threshold flags let you distinguish merely observed alternatives from alternatives common enough to recur in the population.
metrics.help_tip: Whether this site contains any amino acid other than the most common one, even at very low frequency.

metrics.plain_language: Whether the second most common amino acid at this locus has at least 1% frequency.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank the fractional amino-acid frequencies. The locus is classed as polymorphic at the 1% threshold when the second most common residue reaches at least 1%.
metrics.interpretation: True means the locus passes this polymorphism threshold. The 'any' threshold is sensitive to single rare observations; 1% and 5% thresholds require progressively more common alternatives.
metrics.example: If the second residue frequency is 1.2%, this flag is true under the stated threshold. A locus with a second residue at 0.8% fails the ≥1% rule and therefore also fails the ≥5% rule.
metrics.example_interpretation: Threshold flags let you distinguish merely observed alternatives from alternatives common enough to recur in the population.
metrics.help_tip: Whether this site has an alternative amino acid at 1% frequency or higher. This filters out alternatives rarer than the chosen threshold.

metrics.plain_language: Whether the second most common amino acid at this locus has at least 5% frequency.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank the fractional amino-acid frequencies. The locus is classed as polymorphic at the 5% threshold when the second most common residue reaches at least 5%.
metrics.interpretation: True means the locus passes this polymorphism threshold. The 'any' threshold is sensitive to single rare observations; 1% and 5% thresholds require progressively more common alternatives.
metrics.example: If the second residue frequency is 6%, this flag is true under the stated threshold. A locus with a second residue at 0.8% fails the ≥1% rule and therefore also fails the ≥5% rule.
metrics.example_interpretation: Threshold flags let you distinguish merely observed alternatives from alternatives common enough to recur in the population.
metrics.help_tip: Whether this site has an alternative amino acid at 5% frequency or higher. This filters out alternatives rarer than the chosen threshold.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with an explicit missing '-' call at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Divide the number of samples with a missing '-' call at this locus by the total number of selected samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower is better. This isolates explicit missing calls and does not include unresolved non-missing calls.
metrics.example: If 25 of 1,000 samples have '-', the missing rate is 2.5%.
metrics.example_interpretation: One sample in forty lacks a call entirely at this locus.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with a missing call at this site. Lower values mean better data coverage.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of all selected samples that have a callable mixed call, such as [A/V], at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Divide the number of selected samples with a callable mixed call at this locus by the total number of selected samples, including samples that are missing or unresolved in the denominator.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean mixed calls are more prevalent in the cohort. Missing/non-callable samples remain in the denominator, so this can be lower than the mixed fraction among callable samples.
metrics.example: If 100 samples include 10 mixed callable calls and 20 non-callable calls, the all-sample mixed fraction is 10/100 = 10%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Ten percent of the whole cohort has a mixed call at this locus.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of all selected samples with a mixed amino-acid call at this site. Higher values mean mixed calls are more common in the cohort.

metrics.plain_language: Among samples with a callable result at this locus, the fraction whose call is mixed, such as [A/V].
metrics.technical_definition: Look only at callable samples at this locus and divide the number with a mixed call by the total number of callable samples.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean more ambiguity or mixed infection among the usable calls. Because non-callable samples are excluded, this can exceed the all-sample mixed fraction.
metrics.example: If 100 samples include 80 callable calls, of which 10 are mixed, the callable mixed fraction is 10/80 = 12.5%; the all-sample mixed fraction is 10%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Mixed calls make up one eighth of the usable calls, even though they occur in one tenth of all selected samples.
metrics.help_tip: Among samples with a callable result at this site, the fraction with a mixed amino-acid call. This separates mixed calls from missing or unresolved data.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples with a callable result at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Count selected samples whose call at this locus is neither missing nor unresolved.
metrics.interpretation: Higher counts mean more usable evidence, but depend on cohort size.
metrics.example: If 970 of 1,000 selected samples are callable, the count is 970.
metrics.example_interpretation: Most of the cohort contributes usable residue information.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected samples with a usable amino-acid call at this site. More callable samples provide stronger support for frequency estimates.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples with an explicit missing '-' call at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Count selected samples whose call at this locus is marked missing ('-').
metrics.interpretation: Lower is better, but the raw count depends on cohort size.
metrics.example: If 25 of 1,000 samples are missing, the count is 25.
metrics.example_interpretation: Twenty-five samples contribute no call at this locus.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected samples with a missing call at this site. Lower values mean better coverage, but raw counts depend on cohort size.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples with a callable mixed call, such as [A/V], at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Count selected samples with a callable mixed call containing more than one possible canonical amino acid.
metrics.interpretation: Higher counts mean more mixed-call evidence, but depend on cohort size.
metrics.example: If 10 of 1,000 samples have [A/V] or another mixed callable state, the count is 10.
metrics.example_interpretation: Ten samples have multiple possible residues at the locus.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected samples with a callable mixed amino-acid call at this site. This can indicate mixed infections or within-sample ambiguity.

metrics.plain_language: The number of callable/represented calls that cannot contribute a canonical amino-acid residue to the allele-frequency calculation.
metrics.technical_definition: Count calls that are present but cannot be represented as one or more canonical amino-acid alleles under the database call rules.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean more calls fall outside the canonical residue-frequency model. The raw count depends on cohort size.
metrics.example: If 1,000 selected samples contain 4 such calls, the metric is 4.
metrics.example_interpretation: Four calls are represented but cannot be assigned fractional weight to standard amino-acid alleles.
metrics.help_tip: The number of callable observations that cannot be assigned to canonical amino-acid residues for frequency counting. Higher values mean more callable data are still unusable for allele frequencies.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples whose call is missing or unresolved at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Add the number of missing calls and unresolved non-missing calls at this locus.
metrics.interpretation: Lower is better. This is the total number of samples that cannot contribute a resolved callable call.
metrics.example: If 25 calls are missing and 5 are unresolved, the non-callable count is 30.
metrics.example_interpretation: Thirty samples lack a usable resolved call at the locus.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected samples with a missing or unresolved call at this site. Lower values mean more usable data.

metrics.plain_language: The number of different canonical amino acids represented at this locus, including residues that appear inside mixed calls.
metrics.technical_definition: Collect all canonical amino acids seen in callable samples at this locus, including residues present inside mixed calls, and count the distinct residues.
metrics.interpretation: 1 indicates complete observed residue richness of one; larger values mean more residue types are present, but do not reflect their frequencies.
metrics.example: Calls A, A, [A/V], and V contain two observed residues: A and V.
metrics.example_interpretation: The locus has two residue types, even though one appears partly through a mixed call.
metrics.help_tip: The number of different canonical amino acids seen at this site, including residues present inside mixed calls. More residues mean greater amino-acid richness.

metrics.plain_language: The number of amino-acid types at this locus whose fractional frequency is at least 1%.
metrics.technical_definition: Using fractional amino-acid frequencies, count how many residues reach at least 1% frequency at this locus.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean multiple residue types reach a non-trivial frequency. This is less sensitive to extremely rare residues than total observed residue richness.
metrics.example: If residue frequencies are A=92%, V=6%, T=1.5%, and G=0.5%, the ≥1% count is 3.
metrics.example_interpretation: Only residues meeting the 1% threshold contribute, so very rare alternatives are ignored.
metrics.help_tip: The number of amino acids at this site reaching at least 1% frequency. This counts common enough residue types while ignoring rarer ones.

metrics.plain_language: The number of amino-acid types at this locus whose fractional frequency is at least 5%.
metrics.technical_definition: Using fractional amino-acid frequencies, count how many residues reach at least 5% frequency at this locus.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean multiple residue types reach a non-trivial frequency. This is less sensitive to extremely rare residues than total observed residue richness.
metrics.example: If residue frequencies are A=92%, V=6%, T=1.5%, and G=0.5%, the ≥5% count is 2.
metrics.example_interpretation: Only residues meeting the 5% threshold contribute, so very rare alternatives are ignored.
metrics.help_tip: The number of amino acids at this site reaching at least 5% frequency. This counts common enough residue types while ignoring rarer ones.

metrics.plain_language: The number of QC-pass samples contributing to this metric in the current stratum.
metrics.technical_definition: Count the QC-pass samples included in the currently selected population or geographic stratum.
metrics.interpretation: Larger sample sizes usually make frequency estimates more stable, but sample count is not itself a measure of conservation or quality.
metrics.example: If the current country/year stratum contains 1,250 QC-pass samples, this metric is 1,250.
metrics.example_interpretation: All percentages and counts for this stratum should be interpreted in the context of these 1,250 contributing samples.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected QC-passing samples contributing to this site. Use it to judge how much sample support underlies the other metrics.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples with exactly one canonical amino acid at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Count selected samples with exactly one canonical amino acid at this locus. Mixed, missing, unresolved, and non-allelic ambiguous calls are excluded.
metrics.interpretation: Higher counts mean more directly resolved evidence, but depend on cohort size.
metrics.example: If 900 of 1,000 samples have one canonical residue, this metric is 900.
metrics.example_interpretation: Nine out of ten samples provide an unambiguous residue.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected samples with one clear canonical amino acid at this site. These are the simplest calls to interpret directly.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples with a non-missing unresolved call at this locus.
metrics.technical_definition: Count selected samples with an unresolved call at this locus, excluding calls already classified as missing.
metrics.interpretation: Lower is better. These calls contain some sequence state but cannot be resolved into the standard callable representation.
metrics.example: If 5 of 1,000 samples are unresolved, the count is 5.
metrics.example_interpretation: Five samples are not missing, but still cannot contribute a resolved amino-acid call.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected samples with a non-missing but unresolved call at this site. Lower values mean fewer ambiguous technical calls.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples whose call at this locus is missing or unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: Add missing and unresolved calls at this locus, then divide by the total number of selected samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower is better. It gives the total fraction of the cohort without a usable call at the locus.
metrics.example: If 30 of 1,000 samples are missing or unresolved, the non-callable rate is 3%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Usable calls are available for 97% of the selected cohort.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples whose call at this site is missing or unresolved. Lower values mean more samples provide usable residue information.

metrics.display_name: Shannon Entropy, Normalized to 20 Amino Acids
metrics.plain_language: Shannon entropy scaled against the theoretical maximum for 20 equally frequent amino acids, giving a fixed 0–1 scale.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate residue Shannon entropy H and divide it by ln(20), the entropy expected if all 20 standard amino acids were equally frequent. This places the value on a fixed 0-to-1 scale.
metrics.interpretation: 0 means one residue has all the frequency. 1 would require all 20 amino acids to be equally frequent. Because the denominator is fixed, ordinary biallelic variation remains well below 1.
metrics.example: A 50/50 two-residue locus has H = 0.693 and normalized entropy 0.693/ln(20) ≈ 0.231. Even perfect balance between two residues therefore occupies only 23% of the 20-residue maximum.
metrics.example_interpretation: This fixed scale reflects both how many residue types exist and how balanced they are relative to the full amino-acid alphabet.
metrics.help_tip: Site diversity on a fixed 0–1 scale relative to the maximum possible diversity across all 20 amino acids. 0 means one residue only; larger values mean more diverse residue frequencies.

metrics.display_name: Shannon Entropy, Normalized to Observed Residues
metrics.plain_language: Shannon entropy scaled to the maximum possible for the number of residue types actually observed at this locus. This is an evenness measure.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate residue Shannon entropy H and divide it by ln(S), where S is the number of amino acids actually observed at the locus. This compares the observed distribution with the maximum entropy possible for those observed residues.
