metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 mean the observed residues have similar frequencies; lower values mean one or a few dominate. Unlike the 20-residue normalization, it does not penalize a locus simply for having few residue types.
metrics.example: For four observed residues, 25% each gives 1.00. The same four residues at 70%, 10%, 10%, 10% give about 0.68.
metrics.example_interpretation: Both loci have four residue types, but only the first distributes frequency evenly across them.
metrics.help_tip: How evenly diversity is distributed among the amino acids actually observed at this site. Values near 1 mean the observed residues have similar frequencies; lower values indicate dominance.

metrics.plain_language: Shows how evenly the observed amino acids share the total frequency, scaled from 0 toward 1. It asks about balance, not simply how many types exist.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate Shannon diversity H for the observed amino acids, then divide it by ln(S), where S is the number of observed types. This rescales diversity relative to the maximum possible value if those observed types were equally frequent.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 mean the observed amino acids are similarly frequent. Lower values mean one or a few types dominate. Two regions can have the same number of observed types but very different evenness.
metrics.example: With four types at 25% each, Pielou evenness is 1.00. With the same four types at 70%, 10%, 10%, 10%, it is about 0.68.
metrics.example_interpretation: Both examples have four observed types, but the first is perfectly balanced whereas the second is strongly dominated by one type.
metrics.help_tip: How evenly the observed amino acids are represented. 1 means all observed types are equally frequent; lower values mean some types are much more common than others.

metrics.plain_language: The fractional frequency of the 3D7 amino acid at this locus. Mixed calls containing the 3D7 residue contribute partial weight.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate fractional amino-acid weights, splitting a mixed call equally among its possible canonical residues. The reference-residue frequency is the 3D7 residue's weight divided by the total callable allele weight.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 mean the 3D7 residue is highly representative of the selected samples; low values mean alternative residues dominate.
metrics.example: If 3D7 is A and the calls are A and [A/V], A receives weight 1.5 of 2 total, so the reference frequency is 75%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The reference residue is common, but one quarter of the fractional allele weight supports the alternative V.
metrics.help_tip: How common the 3D7 reference amino acid is at this site. Mixed calls contribute partial weight when they include the reference residue.

metrics.plain_language: The fractional frequency of the second most common amino acid at this locus—the strongest alternative to the leading residue.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate fractional frequencies for all observed amino acids, rank them from highest to lowest, and report the second highest value.
metrics.interpretation: Near 0 means the locus is strongly dominated by one residue. Larger values indicate a substantial alternative and therefore weaker residue-level conservation.
metrics.example: A locus with A=98% and V=2% has second-residue frequency 2%; A=60% and V=40% gives 40%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Both loci have two residues, but the 60/40 locus has a much stronger alternative and is much less conserved.
metrics.help_tip: The frequency of the second most common amino acid at this site. This is a simple measure of how strong the main alternative to the consensus residue is.

metrics.plain_language: Summarizes diversity by combining how many amino acids are observed with how evenly their frequencies are distributed. More types and a more even distribution both increase the value.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate H = −Σ(p × ln p) from the positive frequencies of the observed amino acids, using the natural logarithm. Both the number of types and how evenly they are represented affect the value.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean greater diversity, but the number is not itself a count and its maximum depends on how many types are present. For a more intuitive scale, use the corresponding effective-number metric where available.
metrics.example: Two equally frequent types (50%/50%) give H = 0.693 nats. Four equally frequent types give H = 1.386. Two types at 90%/10% give only H ≈ 0.325.
metrics.example_interpretation: Shannon diversity increases both when more types are present and when frequencies become more balanced.
metrics.help_tip: A diversity score for amino acids at this site. It rises when more residues are present and when their frequencies are more even; 0 means only one residue is observed.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with a non-missing call that cannot be resolved into the standard amino-acid representation.
metrics.technical_definition: Divide the number of unresolved non-missing calls at this locus by the total number of selected samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower is better. This measures unresolved evidence separately from explicit missing '-' calls.
metrics.example: If 5 of 1,000 samples have unresolved non-missing calls, the unresolved rate is 0.5%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Only one sample in 200 is unresolved at this locus.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with a non-missing but unresolved call at this site. Lower values mean fewer ambiguous technical calls.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of all selected samples whose full peptide pattern exactly matches the site-by-site consensus built from all samples. Unlike the complete-sequence consensus, this version keeps missing calls in the calculation, so '-' can become the consensus state at a position.
metrics.technical_definition: The consensus is built one position at a time using all selected samples. Missing calls are allowed to compete with amino acids, while a valid mixed call such as [A/V] contributes half to A and half to V. After the consensus pattern has been assembled, its frequency is the proportion of all normalized sample patterns that match that pattern exactly.
metrics.interpretation: A high value means one missing-aware pattern is common across the whole sample set. Interpret it together with call rate and missingness: a high frequency can reflect genuine sequence conservation, but it can also be influenced by a recurring missing-data pattern.
metrics.example: Suppose the all-sample consensus peptide is A-K--V and 35 of 100 selected samples have exactly A-K--V. The metric is 35%. If '-' is the most common state at one position, that missing state is retained in the consensus.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, just over one third of all samples share the exact missing-aware consensus pattern. The value should not be read as 35% complete-sequence conservation because missing calls are part of the pattern.
metrics.help_tip: How often the all-sample, missing-aware consensus peptide is actually observed. Higher values mean one overall pattern is common, but check missingness because '-' can be part of that pattern.

metrics.plain_language: Among complete peptides only, the fraction that exactly match the sequence made by taking the most common amino acid at each position. That site-by-site consensus does not have to be an observed peptide.
metrics.technical_definition: First build the site-by-site consensus peptide from callable amino-acid evidence. Then, among complete peptide observations only, calculate the proportion that match that consensus sequence exactly.
metrics.interpretation: A high value means one consensus peptide represents a large share of the complete data. A value of 0 can occur when the site-wise consensus is a mosaic that no sample actually carries, so interpret it together with the top observed peptide frequency.
metrics.example: Suppose 100 samples are selected, 90 have a complete peptide, and the site-wise consensus is observed in 72 of those 90. The metric is 72/90 = 80%. If the consensus sequence is not present among the 90 complete observations, the value is 0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: An 80% value says the consensus sequence itself is very representative of complete observations. It does not say that 80% of all selected samples are complete.
metrics.help_tip: How often the site-by-site consensus sequence is actually observed as a complete peptide. High values mean the consensus represents many complete observations; 0 can mean that consensus combination is never observed.

metrics.plain_language: Turns Shannon diversity into an intuitive count: the number of equally common peptides that would have the same diversity as the observed frequency distribution.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate Shannon diversity from the frequencies of complete peptides, then convert it to an effective count using exp(H). The result is the number of equally frequent peptides that would give the same Shannon diversity.
metrics.interpretation: 1 means essentially one peptide is present. Larger values mean greater diversity. Unlike the raw number of observed peptides, rare types contribute only in proportion to their frequency, so a long tail of very rare types does not inflate the value as strongly.
metrics.example: Four equally common peptides (25%, 25%, 25%, 25%) give an effective number of 4. If the same four peptides occur at 70%, 10%, 10%, and 10%, the effective number falls to about 2.56.
metrics.example_interpretation: Both examples contain four observed peptides, but the second behaves, in diversity terms, more like about 2.6 equally common peptides because one type dominates.
metrics.help_tip: Diversity translated into an intuitive number of equally common peptides. A value of 4 means the observed diversity is equivalent to four peptides occurring at 25% each; higher means more diversity.

metrics.plain_language: The number of equally common peptides that would give the same Simpson diversity as the observed distribution. It emphasizes common types more strongly than the Shannon effective number.
metrics.technical_definition: Using complete peptides, square each frequency and add the squared values. The reciprocal of that sum, 1/Σp², is the effective Simpson count. This gives more weight to common peptides than to rare ones.
metrics.interpretation: 1 means one peptide dominates completely; larger values mean more diversity. Because frequencies are squared, common peptides have more influence and very rare types have relatively little effect.
metrics.example: Four equally common peptides give 1/(4 × 0.25²) = 4. With frequencies 70%, 10%, 10%, 10%, the value is 1/(0.70² + 3×0.10²) ≈ 1.92.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 70/10/10/10 distribution still contains four peptides, but by this dominance-sensitive measure it behaves like only about 1.9 equally common peptides.
metrics.help_tip: The effective number of common peptides, with extra weight on the most frequent ones. A value of 2 means the distribution behaves roughly like two equally common peptides; higher means more diversity.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples whose entire peptide window is an unambiguous canonical amino-acid sequence.
metrics.technical_definition: Count selected samples whose peptide window is complete and unambiguous at every position, then divide by the total number of selected samples.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean complete peptide sequences are available for more samples, strengthening complete-peptide frequency and diversity estimates.
metrics.example: If 1,000 samples are selected and 860 have a complete peptide, the fraction is 86%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Complete-peptide metrics use a large majority of the cohort here, but 14% of samples are excluded from those complete-sequence calculations.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with a fully resolved peptide: every position is one unambiguous amino acid. Higher values mean more samples can be compared as exact peptide sequences.

metrics.display_name: Samples with an Incomplete or Mixed Peptide
metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples whose peptide window contains at least one missing, unresolved, or mixed call.
metrics.technical_definition: Count selected samples whose peptide contains at least one missing, unresolved, or mixed position, then divide by the total number of selected samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values are better for complete-peptide analyses. This complements 'Samples with a Complete Peptide' and includes both non-callable and mixed-call causes.
metrics.example: If 1,000 samples are selected and 140 contain at least one missing, unresolved, or mixed position, the fraction is 14%; the complete-peptide fraction is 86%.
metrics.example_interpretation: One in seven samples cannot contribute a fully unambiguous peptide sequence, although some may still be fully callable if the only issue is a mixed call.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples whose peptide contains at least one missing, unresolved, or mixed position. Lower values mean more samples have an exact peptide sequence.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥1 missing call within the window.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count the missing '-' calls in the peptide window. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 1 missing call.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean missing data affect fewer samples. Thresholded versions help distinguish occasional isolated missing calls from samples with more substantial missingness.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 12 contain ≥1 missing call, the value is 12%. A stricter threshold can only stay the same or decrease.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 12% means 88% of selected samples do not meet this missingness threshold.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 1 missing call in the peptide window. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥2 missing calls within the window.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count the missing '-' calls in the peptide window. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 2 missing calls.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean missing data affect fewer samples. Thresholded versions help distinguish occasional isolated missing calls from samples with more substantial missingness.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 12 contain ≥2 missing calls, the value is 12%. A stricter threshold can only stay the same or decrease.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 12% means 88% of selected samples do not meet this missingness threshold.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 2 missing calls in the peptide window. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥5 missing calls within the window.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count the missing '-' calls in the peptide window. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 5 missing calls.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean missing data affect fewer samples. Thresholded versions help distinguish occasional isolated missing calls from samples with more substantial missingness.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 12 contain ≥5 missing calls, the value is 12%. A stricter threshold can only stay the same or decrease.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 12% means 88% of selected samples do not meet this missingness threshold.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 5 missing calls in the peptide window. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with >5 missing calls within the window.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count the missing '-' calls in the peptide window. The metric is the proportion of samples with more than 5 missing calls.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean missing data affect fewer samples. Thresholded versions help distinguish occasional isolated missing calls from samples with more substantial missingness.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 12 contain >5 missing calls, the value is 12%. A stricter threshold can only stay the same or decrease.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 12% means 88% of selected samples do not meet this missingness threshold.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with more than 5 missing calls in the peptide window. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥1 mixed callable call within the window. A mixed call records more than one possible amino acid, such as [A/V], rather than being missing.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count callable positions in the peptide window that contain more than one possible amino acid. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 1 mixed call.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean mixed infection or call ambiguity affects more samples at this threshold. Mixed calls remain callable and are therefore different from missing or unresolved calls.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 18 contain ≥1 mixed callable call, the value is 18%. A threshold of ≥5 mixed calls would normally be much lower than a threshold of ≥1.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, mixed calls are present at this level in 18% of samples; the metric does not say that 18% of individual positions are mixed.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 1 mixed amino-acid call in the peptide window. Higher values mean mixed calls affect more samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥2 mixed callable calls within the window. A mixed call records more than one possible amino acid, such as [A/V], rather than being missing.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count callable positions in the peptide window that contain more than one possible amino acid. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 2 mixed calls.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean mixed infection or call ambiguity affects more samples at this threshold. Mixed calls remain callable and are therefore different from missing or unresolved calls.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 18 contain ≥2 mixed callable calls, the value is 18%. A threshold of ≥5 mixed calls would normally be much lower than a threshold of ≥1.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, mixed calls are present at this level in 18% of samples; the metric does not say that 18% of individual positions are mixed.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 2 mixed amino-acid calls in the peptide window. Higher values mean mixed calls affect more samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥5 mixed callable calls within the window. A mixed call records more than one possible amino acid, such as [A/V], rather than being missing.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count callable positions in the peptide window that contain more than one possible amino acid. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 5 mixed calls.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean mixed infection or call ambiguity affects more samples at this threshold. Mixed calls remain callable and are therefore different from missing or unresolved calls.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 18 contain ≥5 mixed callable calls, the value is 18%. A threshold of ≥5 mixed calls would normally be much lower than a threshold of ≥1.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, mixed calls are present at this level in 18% of samples; the metric does not say that 18% of individual positions are mixed.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 5 mixed amino-acid calls in the peptide window. Higher values mean mixed calls affect more samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with >5 mixed callable calls within the window. A mixed call records more than one possible amino acid, such as [A/V], rather than being missing.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count callable positions in the peptide window that contain more than one possible amino acid. The metric is the proportion of samples with more than 5 mixed calls.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean mixed infection or call ambiguity affects more samples at this threshold. Mixed calls remain callable and are therefore different from missing or unresolved calls.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 18 contain >5 mixed callable calls, the value is 18%. A threshold of ≥5 mixed calls would normally be much lower than a threshold of ≥1.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, mixed calls are present at this level in 18% of samples; the metric does not say that 18% of individual positions are mixed.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with more than 5 mixed amino-acid calls in the peptide window. Higher values mean mixed calls affect more samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥1 non-callable position in the window. Non-callable positions are missing or unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count positions in the peptide window that are missing or unresolved. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 1 non-callable position.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more samples have usable sequence information across the region. This combines missing and unresolved calls into one sample-level measure.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 15 contain ≥1 non-callable position, the value is 15%; the other 85 samples fall below that non-callable threshold.
metrics.example_interpretation: This tells you how many samples are affected, not how many total positions are non-callable.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 1 non-callable positions (missing or unresolved) in the peptide window. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥2 non-callable positions in the window. Non-callable positions are missing or unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count positions in the peptide window that are missing or unresolved. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 2 non-callable positions.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more samples have usable sequence information across the region. This combines missing and unresolved calls into one sample-level measure.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 15 contain ≥2 non-callable positions, the value is 15%; the other 85 samples fall below that non-callable threshold.
metrics.example_interpretation: This tells you how many samples are affected, not how many total positions are non-callable.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 2 non-callable positions (missing or unresolved) in the peptide window. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with ≥5 non-callable positions in the window. Non-callable positions are missing or unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count positions in the peptide window that are missing or unresolved. The metric is the proportion of samples with at least 5 non-callable positions.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more samples have usable sequence information across the region. This combines missing and unresolved calls into one sample-level measure.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 15 contain ≥5 non-callable positions, the value is 15%; the other 85 samples fall below that non-callable threshold.
metrics.example_interpretation: This tells you how many samples are affected, not how many total positions are non-callable.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with at least 5 non-callable positions (missing or unresolved) in the peptide window. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of selected samples with >5 non-callable positions in the window. Non-callable positions are missing or unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: For each selected sample, count positions in the peptide window that are missing or unresolved. The metric is the proportion of samples with more than 5 non-callable positions.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more samples have usable sequence information across the region. This combines missing and unresolved calls into one sample-level measure.
metrics.example: If 100 samples are selected and 15 contain >5 non-callable positions, the value is 15%; the other 85 samples fall below that non-callable threshold.
metrics.example_interpretation: This tells you how many samples are affected, not how many total positions are non-callable.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of selected samples with more than 5 non-callable positions (missing or unresolved) in the peptide window. Lower values mean this issue affects fewer samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of amino-acid positions in the window where the second most common residue has any detectable frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the peptide window, identify the second most common amino acid using fractional residue frequencies. A position is counted as polymorphic when that second residue has any non-zero frequency; the metric is the fraction of positions that meet this rule.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position window, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. The corresponding fractions are 16%, 10%, and 4%; for this metric the relevant value is 8/50 = 16%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of positions in the peptide window where any alternative amino acid is observed, even if very rare. Higher values mean polymorphism is spread across more positions.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of amino-acid positions in the window where the second most common residue has at least 1% frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the peptide window, identify the second most common amino acid using fractional residue frequencies. A position is counted as polymorphic when that second residue has at least 1% frequency; the metric is the fraction of positions that meet this rule.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position window, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. The corresponding fractions are 16%, 10%, and 4%; for this metric the relevant value is 5/50 = 10%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of positions in the peptide window where an alternative amino acid reaches at least 1% frequency. This ignores rarer alternatives and highlights more established variation.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of amino-acid positions in the window where the second most common residue has at least 5% frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the peptide window, identify the second most common amino acid using fractional residue frequencies. A position is counted as polymorphic when that second residue has at least 5% frequency; the metric is the fraction of positions that meet this rule.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position window, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. The corresponding fractions are 16%, 10%, and 4%; for this metric the relevant value is 2/50 = 4%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of positions in the peptide window where an alternative amino acid reaches at least 5% frequency. This ignores rarer alternatives and highlights more established variation.

metrics.display_name: Fraction of Sites with a Singleton Residue
metrics.plain_language: The fraction of positions in the window where at least one amino acid is seen in exactly one selected sample. Presence inside a mixed call still counts as presence in that one sample.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the peptide window, check whether any amino acid is present in exactly one sample. A residue seen inside a mixed call still counts as present in that sample. The metric is the fraction of positions containing at least one such singleton residue.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean rare, sample-specific amino-acid variants are spread across more positions. Singleton-rich regions can look polymorphic even when recurrent variants are uncommon.
metrics.example: If a 50-position window has singleton residues at 6 positions, the fraction is 6/50 = 12%. A V seen only once inside [A/V] still makes that site singleton-positive; V seen in two samples does not.
metrics.example_interpretation: This highlights the rarest end of the variation spectrum and complements the ≥1% or ≥5% polymorphism metrics.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of positions in the peptide window that contain an amino acid seen in only one sample. Higher values mean rare one-off variants are spread across more positions.

metrics.display_name: Share of Distinct Peptide Patterns That Are Complete
metrics.plain_language: Among all distinct normalized peptide patterns observed—including patterns with missing, unresolved, or mixed calls—the fraction that are complete unambiguous peptide sequences.
metrics.technical_definition: First count the distinct normalized peptide patterns seen across all samples. Then calculate what fraction of those distinct patterns are complete, unambiguous canonical peptide sequences.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean most distinct observed patterns represent fully resolved peptides. Lower values mean pattern richness is substantially driven by incomplete or mixed-call patterns.
metrics.example: If 40 distinct normalized peptide patterns are observed and 30 are complete peptides, the fraction is 30/40 = 75%.
metrics.example_interpretation: One quarter of the distinct patterns arise from missing, unresolved, or mixed calls rather than complete peptide sequences.
metrics.help_tip: Among all distinct peptide call patterns observed, the fraction that are fully resolved sequences. Higher values mean fewer distinct patterns are created by missing, unresolved, or mixed calls.

metrics.plain_language: Within the peptide window, the largest mixed-call fraction observed at any single locus among callable samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each position in the peptide window, calculate the fraction of callable samples that have a mixed call. The metric is the largest of those position-specific fractions.
metrics.interpretation: A high value flags a local hotspot of mixed calls even when the average across the peptide is low. One problematic locus is enough to make this metric high.
metrics.example: If locus-level mixed fractions across a 5-AA peptide are 1%, 2%, 3%, 18%, and 2%, the metric is 18%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Most positions are clean, but one position has mixed calls in nearly one fifth of callable samples.
metrics.help_tip: The highest mixed-call fraction at any single site in the peptide window. A high value can reveal one problematic or highly mixed position even when the rest of the window is clean.

metrics.plain_language: The average pairwise amino-acid difference between complete peptides, expressed as a fraction of the window length so regions of different lengths are comparable.
metrics.technical_definition: Compare every pair of complete peptides, count the amino-acid positions at which each pair differs, and average those distances. Divide that mean by the peptide window length so values from regions of different lengths are directly comparable.
metrics.interpretation: 0 means complete sequences are identical. A value of 0.10 means a typical pair differs at about 10% of positions. This is more comparable across block/window lengths than the raw pairwise distance.
metrics.example: An average of 2 differences in a 20-AA region gives 2/20 = 0.10. The same 2 differences in a 100-AA region give 0.02.
metrics.example_interpretation: The absolute number of differences is the same, but variation is much denser in the 20-AA region.
metrics.help_tip: The average pairwise amino-acid difference expressed as a fraction of sequence length. For example, 0.10 means two complete peptides differ at about 10% of positions on average.

metrics.plain_language: For two randomly chosen complete peptides, the average number of amino-acid positions at which their sequences differ.
metrics.technical_definition: Compare every unordered pair of complete peptide observations, count how many amino-acid positions differ in each pair, and take the average number of differences.
metrics.interpretation: 0 means all complete peptides are identical. Larger values mean complete sequences differ at more positions on average. Because this is an absolute count, longer regions can naturally have larger values.
metrics.example: If three complete peptides have pairwise distances of 1, 2, and 3 amino acids, the mean distance is (1+2+3)/3 = 2 AA.
metrics.example_interpretation: A value of 2 means a typical pair of complete peptides differs at about two positions.
metrics.help_tip: The average number of amino-acid positions at which two complete peptides differ. Larger values mean the sequences are typically farther apart.

metrics.plain_language: For each sample, calculate the fraction of positions in the window that are callable, then average those fractions across samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, calculate the proportion of positions in the peptide window that are callable, then average those per-sample proportions.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean samples are, on average, well covered by usable calls. Because each sample contributes equally, one sample does not get extra weight simply because it has more callable positions.
metrics.example: If three samples have call rates of 100%, 90%, and 80%, the mean sample call rate is 90%.
metrics.example_interpretation: A 90% value means the average sample has callable information at about nine out of every ten positions.
metrics.help_tip: For each sample, the fraction of positions in the peptide window that are callable, averaged across samples. Higher values mean more complete sequence information overall.

metrics.plain_language: For each sample, the fraction of window positions marked missing (-), averaged across all selected samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, calculate the proportion of positions in the peptide window marked missing ('-'), then average those proportions across samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values are better. A value of 0 means no missing calls; 0.05 means the average sample is missing 5% of positions.
metrics.example: If three samples have missing fractions of 0%, 5%, and 10%, the average missing fraction is 5%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The average sample is missing about one position in twenty, although individual samples may be better or worse.
metrics.help_tip: The average fraction of positions in the peptide window that are explicitly missing in each sample. Lower values mean less missing sequence data.

metrics.display_name: Average Mixed Fraction per Sample (Callable Positions)
metrics.plain_language: For each sample, calculate what fraction of its callable window positions are mixed calls such as [A/V], then average those fractions across samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, look only at callable positions in the peptide window and calculate what fraction are mixed calls. The reported value is the average of those per-sample fractions.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean mixed calls occupy more of the callable sequence in a typical sample. Each sample contributes equally, regardless of how many callable positions it has.
metrics.example: If two samples have mixed fractions of 0% and 20% among their callable positions, the mean is 10%, even if one sample has many more callable positions than the other.
metrics.example_interpretation: This describes the typical sample. It can differ from the pooled mixed fraction, which gives more weight to samples with more callable positions.
metrics.help_tip: Among callable positions, the average fraction that are mixed within each sample. Higher values mean samples more often contain evidence for multiple amino acids at the same position.

metrics.plain_language: For each sample, the fraction of window positions that are missing or unresolved, averaged across selected samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, calculate the fraction of positions in the peptide window that are missing or unresolved, then average across samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more complete usable sequence information. This is broader than missing fraction because it also counts unresolved calls.
metrics.example: If sample non-callable fractions are 2%, 4%, and 9%, the average is 5%.
metrics.example_interpretation: On average, 5% of positions per sample cannot be used as resolved amino-acid calls.
metrics.help_tip: The average fraction of positions in the peptide window that cannot be used because they are missing or unresolved. Lower values mean cleaner sequence data.

metrics.plain_language: For each sample, the fraction of window positions carrying unresolved non-missing markers such as ! or *, averaged across samples.
metrics.technical_definition: For each sample, calculate the fraction of positions in the peptide window that are unresolved but not missing, then average across samples.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values are better. High values indicate that sequence information is present but cannot be represented as a resolved canonical amino-acid call.
metrics.example: If three samples have unresolved fractions of 0%, 3%, and 6%, the average is 3%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The average sample has unresolved evidence at about 3% of positions, separately from explicitly missing '-' calls.
metrics.help_tip: The average fraction of positions in the peptide window carrying unresolved calls rather than a usable amino acid. Lower values mean fewer ambiguous technical calls.

metrics.plain_language: The call rate of the worst-covered position in the peptide window.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate the call rate separately at every position in the peptide window and report the lowest value. One poorly called position therefore determines the metric.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean every position is well called. Because this is a minimum, a single poorly called locus can lower the whole-window value.
metrics.example: If locus call rates in a 5-AA peptide are 99%, 98%, 97%, 91%, and 99%, the metric is 91%. A filter of ≥90% passes; a filter of ≥95% fails.
metrics.example_interpretation: Even though most positions are near 100% callable, the window is only as strong as its 91% worst position under this metric.
metrics.help_tip: The call rate of the worst-covered site in the peptide window. A value of 0.90 means every position is callable in at least 90% of selected samples.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of all selected samples with the most common normalized peptide pattern, counting complete patterns and patterns that contain missing, unresolved, or mixed calls.
metrics.technical_definition: Treat each selected sample's full peptide call pattern as an observed pattern, including missing, unresolved, or mixed calls. After normalizing their representation, identify the most common pattern and divide its count by the total number of selected samples.
metrics.interpretation: A high value means one exact call pattern is common across the whole selected cohort. Because incomplete patterns are allowed, a high value can sometimes reflect a recurrent missing or mixed-call pattern rather than a common biological sequence.
metrics.example: In 100 samples, suppose the most common pattern occurs 42 times and contains one missing position, while the most common complete peptide occurs 35 times. This metric is 42%, whereas the complete-{seq} frequency metric would be based only on complete observations.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 42% value describes the most repeated observed call pattern, not necessarily the most common fully resolved biological sequence.
metrics.help_tip: The frequency of the most common peptide call pattern when every sample is included, even those with missing or mixed calls. Useful for seeing the dominant observed pattern without requiring complete sequences.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of sample-by-position calls in the window that are callable: neither missing nor unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: Count every sample-by-position call in the peptide window that is neither missing nor unresolved. Mixed calls are included because they are still callable.
metrics.interpretation: Higher counts mean more usable sequence evidence, but the value scales with both cohort size and region length.
metrics.example: With 100 samples and a 20-position window, there are 2,000 possible calls. If 1,940 are callable, this metric is 1,940.
metrics.example_interpretation: The dataset provides usable amino-acid information for 97% of all possible sample-by-position calls in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of usable amino-acid calls across all samples and positions in the peptide window. Larger counts usually mean more data, but also reflect cohort and region size.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples whose entire window contains only unambiguous canonical amino acids—no missing, unresolved, or mixed calls.
metrics.technical_definition: Count sample observations whose entire peptide window contains one unambiguous canonical amino acid at every position. Any missing, unresolved, or mixed position makes the observation incomplete.
metrics.interpretation: Higher counts provide a larger evidence base for complete-peptide frequency and diversity metrics. The count can be much smaller than n_samples if mixed or incomplete calls are common.
metrics.example: If 1,000 samples are selected and 860 have an unambiguous canonical call at every position, there are 860 complete peptide observations.
metrics.example_interpretation: Complete-peptide metrics are based on these 860 observations, not automatically on all 1,000 samples.
metrics.help_tip: The number of samples with a complete peptide containing only unambiguous amino acids. These observations are used for exact peptide-frequency and diversity calculations.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected samples with no missing or unresolved positions anywhere in the window. Mixed calls are allowed.
metrics.technical_definition: Count sample observations with no missing or unresolved positions anywhere in the peptide window. Mixed calls are allowed because they still contain callable amino-acid information.
metrics.interpretation: This is a less strict completeness measure than complete peptide observations because mixed calls are allowed. A large gap between the two counts points to mixed calls rather than missingness.
metrics.example: If 1,000 samples include 920 fully callable peptides, but only 860 are complete unambiguous peptides, then 60 observations are fully callable yet contain at least one mixed call.
metrics.example_interpretation: The difference between fully callable and fully complete observations helps separate mixed-call ambiguity from missing/unresolved data.
metrics.help_tip: The number of peptide observations with no missing or unresolved positions. Mixed calls are allowed, so this can exceed the number of complete unambiguous peptides.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of calls in the window marked missing (-).
metrics.technical_definition: Count all positions marked missing ('-') across the selected samples and all positions in the peptide window.
metrics.interpretation: Lower is better, but the raw count depends on sample number and region length.
metrics.example: In 2,000 possible sample-by-position calls, 40 missing '-' calls give this metric a value of 40.
metrics.example_interpretation: Forty individual calls are missing; this does not tell you whether they are concentrated in a few samples or spread across many.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of missing calls across the peptide window. Lower counts mean less missing data, but compare counts only across similarly sized cohorts and regions.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of callable positions in the window with more than one possible amino acid, such as [A/V].
metrics.technical_definition: Count all callable positions in the peptide window that contain more than one possible canonical amino acid, such as [A/V].
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean more mixed-call evidence, but the count also grows with cohort size and region length.
metrics.example: If 30 of 1,940 callable sample-by-position calls are mixed, this metric is 30.
metrics.example_interpretation: There are 30 mixed calls in total; the pooled mixed fraction would express this relative to the 1,940 callable calls.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of callable positions containing multiple possible amino acids across the peptide window. Higher counts mean mixed calls are more common, but counts depend on dataset size.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of calls in the window that are missing or unresolved.
metrics.technical_definition: Count all missing calls plus all unresolved non-missing calls across the selected samples and positions in the peptide window.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values mean more usable sequence evidence. The raw count depends on cohort size and region length.
metrics.example: If a window contains 40 missing calls and 10 unresolved calls, the non-callable count is 50.
metrics.example_interpretation: The combined value shows total unusable calls; separate missing and unresolved counts show why they are unusable.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of missing or unresolved calls across the peptide window. Lower counts mean cleaner data, but counts depend on cohort and region size.

metrics.plain_language: The number of selected peptide observations containing at least one missing, unresolved, or mixed call.
metrics.technical_definition: Count selected samples whose peptide window is not a complete unambiguous canonical sequence because at least one position is missing, unresolved, or mixed.
metrics.interpretation: Lower counts mean more samples contribute clean complete peptides. The count depends on cohort size.
metrics.example: Among 1,000 selected samples, if 860 peptides are complete and 140 contain at least one missing, unresolved, or mixed call, this metric is 140.
metrics.example_interpretation: Those 140 observations are excluded from strict complete-peptide sequence-frequency calculations.
metrics.help_tip: The number of peptide observations containing at least one missing, unresolved, or mixed position. Lower values mean more samples have an exact peptide sequence.

metrics.plain_language: The number of QC-pass samples contributing to this metric in the current stratum.
metrics.technical_definition: Count the QC-pass samples included in the currently selected population or geographic stratum.
metrics.interpretation: Larger sample sizes usually make frequency estimates more stable, but sample count is not itself a measure of conservation or quality.
metrics.example: If the current country/year stratum contains 1,250 QC-pass samples, this metric is 1,250.
metrics.example_interpretation: All percentages and counts for this stratum should be interpreted in the context of these 1,250 contributing samples.
metrics.help_tip: The number of selected QC-passing samples contributing to this peptide window. Use it to judge how much sample support underlies the other metrics.

metrics.plain_language: The number of distinct complete peptide types observed in exactly one selected sample.
metrics.technical_definition: Among the distinct complete peptide sequences, count how many are observed in exactly one sample.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a larger rare tail of one-off complete peptides. Singleton counts are especially sensitive to sample size and possible sequencing/calling artefacts.
metrics.example: If 20 distinct complete peptides are observed and 7 occur in only one sample each, this metric is 7.
metrics.example_interpretation: Seven of the observed peptide types are unique to single samples; the remaining 13 occur at least twice.
metrics.help_tip: The number of distinct complete peptide types seen in only one sample. Many singletons can indicate a long tail of rare sequence variants.

metrics.plain_language: The number of amino-acid positions in the window where the second most common residue has any detectable frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the peptide window, look at the second most common amino acid. Count the positions where that alternative residue has any non-zero frequency.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position window, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. For this metric the count is 8.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The number of positions in the peptide window where any alternative amino acid is observed, even if only once. More sites means variation is distributed across more positions.

metrics.plain_language: The number of amino-acid positions in the window where the second most common residue has at least 1% frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the peptide window, look at the second most common amino acid. Count the positions where that alternative residue has at least 1% frequency.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position window, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. For this metric the count is 5.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The number of positions in the peptide window where an alternative amino acid reaches at least 1% frequency. This focuses on variation that is more than extremely rare.

metrics.plain_language: The number of amino-acid positions in the window where the second most common residue has at least 5% frequency. This asks how much of the region is variable, using the chosen frequency threshold.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the peptide window, look at the second most common amino acid. Count the positions where that alternative residue has at least 5% frequency.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean variability is spread across more positions. The 'any frequency' version is very sensitive to rare variants; the 1% and 5% versions progressively focus on more common polymorphism.
metrics.example: In a 50-position window, suppose 8 sites have any alternative residue, 5 have a second residue at ≥1%, and 2 have one at ≥5%. For this metric the count is 2.
metrics.example_interpretation: Comparing thresholds separates rare variation from common variation: many 'any-frequency' sites but few ≥5% sites suggests a long tail of rare alternatives.
metrics.help_tip: The number of positions in the peptide window where an alternative amino acid reaches at least 5% frequency. This focuses on variation that is more than extremely rare.

metrics.plain_language: The number of positions in the window where at least one amino acid is seen in exactly one selected sample. Presence inside a mixed call still counts as presence in that one sample.
metrics.technical_definition: At each position in the peptide window, check whether any amino acid appears in exactly one sample, including appearances inside mixed calls. Count the positions that contain at least one such singleton residue.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean rare, sample-specific amino-acid variants are spread across more positions. Singleton-rich regions can look polymorphic even when recurrent variants are uncommon.
metrics.example: If a 50-position window has singleton residues at 6 positions, the count is 6. A V seen only once inside [A/V] still makes that site singleton-positive; V seen in two samples does not.
metrics.example_interpretation: This highlights the rarest end of the variation spectrum and complements the ≥1% or ≥5% polymorphism metrics.
metrics.help_tip: The number of positions in the peptide window containing an amino acid seen in only one sample. This highlights sites carrying very rare variants.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of sample-by-position calls represented in the window.
metrics.technical_definition: Count all sample-by-position entries in the peptide window. This is the number of selected samples multiplied by the number of positions in the peptide window.
metrics.interpretation: This is mainly a denominator/evidence-size metric rather than a conservation metric.
metrics.example: With 100 selected samples and a 20-position window, there are 100 × 20 = 2,000 total calls.
metrics.example_interpretation: This is the maximum pool from which callable, missing, mixed, and unresolved call counts are drawn.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of sample-by-position calls in the peptide window, before separating callable, missing, mixed, or unresolved calls.

metrics.plain_language: The number of different normalized peptide patterns observed across all selected samples, including complete, missing, unresolved, and mixed-call patterns.
metrics.technical_definition: Represent each sample's full peptide call pattern consistently, including missing, unresolved, and mixed calls, then count how many distinct patterns occur.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean more pattern richness, but some of that richness may reflect missingness or mixed-call structure rather than distinct complete biological peptides.
metrics.example: If 1,000 samples produce 40 distinct normalized patterns but only 25 distinct complete peptides, the additional 15 patterns involve missing, unresolved, or mixed calls.
metrics.example_interpretation: Raw pattern richness is higher than complete-peptide richness because incomplete call patterns create additional states.
metrics.help_tip: The number of distinct peptide call patterns across all samples, including patterns with missing, unresolved, or mixed positions. This shows total observed pattern complexity, not just exact peptides.

metrics.plain_language: The number of different complete peptide sequences observed among selected samples.
metrics.technical_definition: Among complete, unambiguous peptide observations, collapse identical sequences together and count the number of distinct sequences.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean greater observed richness, but this raw count increases with sample size and can be inflated by rare singletons.
metrics.example: If 500 complete observations contain 12 different peptide sequences, this metric is 12. If 8 of those 12 occur only once, richness is high but much of it is rare.
metrics.example_interpretation: A count of 12 tells you how many types were seen, not whether they are common or evenly distributed.
metrics.help_tip: The number of distinct complete peptide sequences observed in the window. More types mean greater peptide richness, although the count also grows with sample size.

metrics.plain_language: The total number of non-missing calls in the window that remain unresolved, for example calls represented by markers such as ! or *.
metrics.technical_definition: Count non-missing calls in the peptide window that are marked unresolved rather than assigned a usable amino-acid state.
metrics.interpretation: Lower values are better. This separates unresolved sequence information from explicit missing '-' calls.
metrics.example: If 2,000 total calls contain 10 unresolved non-missing calls, this metric is 10.
metrics.example_interpretation: Ten positions contain sequence information that cannot be represented as a resolved amino-acid call.
metrics.help_tip: The total number of unresolved, non-missing calls across the peptide window. Lower counts mean fewer ambiguous technical calls.

metrics.plain_language: The probability that two complete peptides drawn from the sample are different, with a small correction for finite sample size.
metrics.technical_definition: Using complete peptides only, calculate 1 − Σp² from their observed frequencies and apply the finite-sample correction n/(n−1). This estimates the probability that two randomly chosen complete peptides are different.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 0 mean most complete observations are the same peptide; values near 1 mean two randomly chosen complete observations are very likely to be different. Hd captures both richness and frequency balance, but it does not tell you how many amino-acid positions differ.
metrics.example: With two peptides at 90% and 10%, the uncorrected value is 1−(0.9²+0.1²)=0.18. At 50% and 50%, it is 0.50. The stored Hd is slightly higher after multiplying by n/(n−1).
metrics.example_interpretation: Two equally common peptides produce much more diversity than a 90/10 split, even though both windows contain exactly two observed types.
metrics.help_tip: The chance that two randomly chosen complete peptides are different. 0 means they are all the same; values closer to 1 mean two random peptides are very likely to differ.

metrics.plain_language: Measures how unevenly frequency is distributed across the observed peptide types. A value of 0 means all observed types are equally frequent; larger values mean a few types dominate.
metrics.technical_definition: Apply the standard Gini coefficient to the positive complete peptide frequencies. Only types that are actually observed are included; absent types with zero frequency are ignored.
metrics.interpretation: Low Gini means the observed peptide types have similar frequencies. High Gini means frequency is concentrated in a small number of types. Unlike a diversity index, Gini focuses specifically on inequality among the types that are present.
metrics.example: Four types at 25%, 25%, 25%, 25% have Gini = 0. Four types at 70%, 10%, 10%, 10% have Gini ≈ 0.45; at 97%, 1%, 1%, 1% it is ≈ 0.72.
metrics.example_interpretation: The number of observed types is unchanged, but the Gini rises as one type becomes increasingly dominant.
metrics.help_tip: How unequal the frequencies of the observed peptides are. 0 means all types are equally common; higher values mean one or a few types dominate.

metrics.plain_language: Shows how evenly the observed peptides share the total frequency, scaled from 0 toward 1. It asks about balance, not simply how many types exist.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate Shannon diversity H for the observed peptides, then divide it by ln(S), where S is the number of observed types. This rescales diversity relative to the maximum possible value if those observed types were equally frequent.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 mean the observed peptides are similarly frequent. Lower values mean one or a few types dominate. Two regions can have the same number of observed types but very different evenness.
metrics.example: With four types at 25% each, Pielou evenness is 1.00. With the same four types at 70%, 10%, 10%, 10%, it is about 0.68.
metrics.example_interpretation: Both examples have four observed types, but the first is perfectly balanced whereas the second is strongly dominated by one type.
metrics.help_tip: How evenly the observed peptides are represented. 1 means all observed types are equally frequent; lower values mean some types are much more common than others.

metrics.plain_language: Across all callable sample-by-position calls in the window, the fraction that are mixed calls such as [A/V].
metrics.technical_definition: Pool all callable sample-by-position calls in the peptide window. The metric is the number of mixed calls divided by the total number of callable calls, so samples with more callable positions contribute more observations.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a larger share of all usable calls are mixed. Samples with more callable positions contribute more calls, unlike the mean per-sample mixed fraction.
metrics.example: Suppose sample A has 100 callable positions with 10 mixed calls and sample B has 10 callable positions with 0 mixed calls. The pooled fraction is 10/110 = 9.1%, while the mean of the two sample fractions is (10%+0%)/2 = 5%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The pooled metric is higher because the sample with more callable data contributes more weight.
metrics.help_tip: The overall share of callable sample-by-position calls in the peptide window that are mixed. Higher values mean mixed infections or ambiguous within-sample residue calls are more common.

metrics.plain_language: Among complete peptides, the fraction that exactly match the 3D7 reference sequence across the whole window.
metrics.technical_definition: Among complete peptide observations only, count those that match the 3D7 reference sequence exactly and divide by the total number of complete observations. Sequences with missing, unresolved, or mixed calls are excluded.
metrics.interpretation: Values near 1 mean the 3D7 peptide is highly representative of the complete observations; low values mean most complete peptides differ from 3D7. This measures reference representativeness, not overall diversity.
metrics.example: If 90 samples have complete peptides and 72 are identical to 3D7, the frequency is 72/90 = 80%. If another 10 selected samples are incomplete, they do not enter this denominator.
metrics.example_interpretation: Here, 3D7 represents four out of five complete observations, but the metric says nothing about how the remaining 20% are distributed among other types.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete peptides that exactly match the 3D7 reference sequence. High values mean the reference form is common in this population.

metrics.plain_language: Summarizes diversity by combining how many peptides are observed with how evenly their frequencies are distributed. More types and a more even distribution both increase the value.
metrics.technical_definition: Calculate H = −Σ(p × ln p) from the positive frequencies of the observed complete peptides, using the natural logarithm. Both the number of types and how evenly they are represented affect the value.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean greater diversity, but the number is not itself a count and its maximum depends on how many types are present. For a more intuitive scale, use the corresponding effective-number metric where available.
metrics.example: Two equally frequent types (50%/50%) give H = 0.693 nats. Four equally frequent types give H = 1.386. Two types at 90%/10% give only H ≈ 0.325.
metrics.example_interpretation: Shannon diversity increases both when more types are present and when frequencies become more balanced.
metrics.help_tip: A diversity score that increases when there are more peptides and when their frequencies are more even. 0 means only one complete peptide is observed; higher values mean greater diversity.

metrics.display_name: Singleton Share of Complete Peptide Types
metrics.plain_language: Among the distinct complete peptide types observed, the fraction that occur in exactly one selected sample.
metrics.technical_definition: Count distinct complete peptide types seen in exactly one sample and divide by the total number of distinct complete peptide types.
metrics.interpretation: High values mean much of the observed richness consists of one-off peptides; low values mean most distinct types recur in multiple samples.
metrics.example: If 20 distinct complete peptides are observed and 7 are singletons, the fraction is 7/20 = 35%.
metrics.example_interpretation: Although 20 types were observed, more than a third of those types are represented by only one sample each.
metrics.help_tip: The fraction of distinct complete peptide types that occur only once. A high value means much of the observed sequence richness consists of rare, one-sample types.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete peptide observations accounted for by the 10 most common complete peptide types.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete peptide types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 10. If fewer than 10 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common peptides covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-peptide frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-10 coverage is 100.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 10 most common complete peptides together represent 100.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete peptide observations covered by the 10 most common peptides together. Higher values mean a small set of sequences captures more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete peptide observations accounted for by the 1 most common complete peptide type.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete peptide types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 1. If fewer than 1 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common peptides covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-peptide frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-1 coverage is 40.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 1 most common complete peptide together represent 40.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete peptide observations explained by the single most common peptide. Higher values mean one sequence covers more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete peptide observations accounted for by the 2 most common complete peptide types.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete peptide types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 2. If fewer than 2 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common peptides covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-peptide frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-2 coverage is 65.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 2 most common complete peptides together represent 65.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete peptide observations covered by the 2 most common peptides together. Higher values mean a small set of sequences captures more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete peptide observations accounted for by the 3 most common complete peptide types.
metrics.technical_definition: Rank complete peptide types from most to least frequent and add the frequencies of the top 3. If fewer than 3 types exist, all available types are included.
metrics.interpretation: Higher values mean a small set of common peptides covers more of the complete observations—useful for assessing how many sequence variants would be needed to cover most samples. Values are cumulative, so top-1 ≤ top-2 ≤ top-3 ≤ top-5 ≤ top-10.
metrics.example: If the leading complete-peptide frequencies are 40%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 5%, 2%, 1%, 1%, 0.5%, and 0.5%, the top-3 coverage is 80.0%.
metrics.example_interpretation: The 3 most common complete peptides together represent 80.0% of complete observations in this example.
metrics.help_tip: The share of complete peptide observations covered by the 3 most common peptides together. Higher values mean a small set of sequences captures more of the population.

metrics.plain_language: The fraction of complete peptide observations accounted for by the 5 most common complete peptide types.

metrics.plain_language: Among complete peptides, the fraction belonging to the single most common observed peptide.
metrics.technical_definition: Among complete peptide observations only, identify the most common distinct sequence and report its frequency. Observations containing missing, unresolved, or mixed calls do not contribute.
metrics.interpretation: A high value means one peptide dominates the complete observations. A low value means the observations are spread across several peptides. The most common peptide is not necessarily the 3D7 or site-wise consensus sequence.
metrics.example: If 90 complete peptides contain 54 copies of type A, 18 of type B, and 18 across other types, the value is 54/90 = 60%. A second window with frequencies 30%, 25%, 20%, … would have a much lower top frequency despite having the same number of complete observations.
metrics.example_interpretation: The first window is dominated by one peptide; the second is more evenly split among several peptides.
metrics.help_tip: The frequency of the single most common complete peptide. A high value means one sequence dominates; a low value means the population is spread across several sequences.
